analysis.one_liner: Closes tax loopholes used by multinational corporations after inversions.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 6 cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand the tax code's rules on 'controlled foreign corporations' — foreign subsidiaries that American-owned multinationals use to hold profits abroad — so that companies that have moved their official headquarters overseas (or structured themselves under a foreign parent) cannot use those structures to dodge taxes on profits parked outside the United States. It also stops a company from shuffling stock to a foreign affiliate to slip below the ownership threshold that triggers these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would bear a smaller share of the tax burden if profitable multinationals could not shield foreign earnings from US tax. Domestic companies that remain US-based and pay full US taxes would also face less competitive disadvantage against inverted rivals.

how_it_helps.text: It counts a broader pool of foreign holdings toward the taxable 'investment of earnings in US property' of controlled foreign corporations when the group's parent is a foreign corporation, so foreign-parented groups cannot move the same earnings out of reach [S3].
It ends a rule that let companies avoid being treated as a controlled foreign corporation through related-party stock transfers, applying the change to transactions after May 17, 2016 [S3].

The CRS summary describes the bill as revising rules for taxing earnings and determining stock ownership of controlled foreign corporations, including prohibiting stock transfers to foreign affiliates to drop below the ownership threshold [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations — particularly those that have inverted or operate under foreign common parents — would pay more US tax on profits they currently structure to avoid. Consumers could see some of those costs passed through in prices.

drawbacks.text: The measure targets structures of a narrow set of companies (foreign-parented groups), so its revenue impact would be limited compared with broader corporate tax reform [S2].
Critics of anti-avoidance rules argue that taxing earnings held abroad can push investment and headquarters decisions further offshore; the bill text does not include analysis of that risk [S3].
The bill was introduced mid-election-year with no Republican cosponsors, giving it no apparent path to a committee vote even before its provisions could be debated [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms the bill is a targeted loophole-closer: it raises revenue from a specific tax-avoidance structure without raising anyone's individual tax rates. The cost falls on the corporations affected, with some possible pass-through to consumers, and the bill is narrow enough that it would not fix the broader incentive to shift profits offshore. Its main weakness is that it died with no committee action, so its provisions were never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sander Levin introduced the bill on May 17, 2016, with six Democratic cosponsors, all Ways and Means Committee members [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; that is the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinationals that use inverted or foreign-parent structures, and the shareholders of those companies, kept the existing tax treatment; no revenue was collected from the structures the bill targeted.

for.name: Sander M. Levin
for.role: US Representative (D-MI), senior Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House

for.name: Chris Van Hollen, Charles Rangel, Jim McDermott, Mike Thompson, Bill Pascrell, Danny K. Davis
for.role: House Ways and Means Committee Democrats

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever held

sides.party_line_note: All 7 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, including Ways and Means members; no Republicans signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Multinational corporations with inverted or foreign-parent structures
industries.note: The bill would tax a pool of foreign earnings these groups currently structure to keep out of the US tax base under section 956 [S3]. Their gain under the status quo is revenue ordinary taxpayers must make up elsewhere.

industries.industry: US-headquartered multinationals that pay full US tax on foreign earnings
industries.note: Closing the avoidance structures reduces the competitive advantage of rivals that keep earnings offshore, bringing the tax playing field closer to even.
